key_terms.meaning: Shear force carried per unit length of wall, q = τt, measured in N/mm; t is wall thickness and τ is shear stress.
The point in the cross-section through which a transverse load must act so the beam bends without twisting; also called flexural centre.
A thin-walled section whose wall centreline does not form a closed loop, so the shear flow starts at zero at each free edge.
The end of a wall where no shear can be carried across the cut, so q = 0 there and the integration starts.
The shear flow computed in the section after it is cut open, before any constant q₀ is added.
An imaginary slit at one point of a closed loop that turns it into an open section and lets the free-edge integration begin.
An unknown uniform shear flow added round the whole loop; its value is fixed by the zero-twist or known-shear-centre condition.
For a closed thin-walled tube under torque T, q = T/(2A), where A is the area enclosed by the wall centreline; q is the same all round.
The area bounded by the centreline of the closed wall, not by the outer surface; it appears squared in the torsion constant.
For a single closed cell, J = 4A²/∮(ds/t), s measured round the wall; the twist rate is dθ/dz = T/(GJ).
One closed loop of a multi-cell box; a two-cell box has two loops sharing a common internal wall.
All cells of one box section twist by the same rate, so θ₁ = θ₂ = … gives one extra equation per pair of cells.
A wall of a box that carries no direct stress, so it contributes only shear flow and torsion, not bending stiffness.
A lumped area in an idealized section that carries all the direct (bending) stress; real booms are stringers and flange upstands.
A thin wall between adjacent booms that carries only shear flow, with the direct stress taken as constant along it.
The extra shear flow caused by the spanwise component of the changing boom load in a tapered beam or wing.
The stress pattern in a thin web that has buckled in shear: load is carried along one diagonal by tension and along the other by compression.
Method for a buckled thin web: the diagonal tension angle α fixes the shear flows in the web and the added loads on the booms.
For an open thin-walled section, J = Σ(bt³/3) over all walls; it grows with the cube of the thickness, so open walls are torsion-weak.

takeaways: Shear flow q is force per unit length of wall, so the wall thickness and the section shape decide both the stress and where the shear centre sits.
A transverse load through the shear centre produces pure bending; a load anywhere else produces bending plus a twisting moment equal to the load times its offset from the shear centre.
In an open section the shear flow is fully determined by statics alone, starting from zero at a free edge and integrating the direct stress gradient round the wall.
A closed section carries an extra unknown constant q₀, so statics is not enough and a compatibility condition such as zero twist or a known shear centre is needed.
Bredt-Batho theory makes the shear flow constant round a closed tube, and it depends on the enclosed area A, so a fat tube is far more efficient than a thin one.
A multi-cell box is solved by cutting each cell, adding one q₀ per cell, and forcing all cells to twist at the same rate.
Idealizing a wing into booms and panels replaces a difficult integral over a curved wall with a short sum over a few areas and lengths.
A tapered beam needs an extra taper shear flow because the boom load changes along the span, and that change has a spanwise component.
A buckled thin web is not a failed web: Wagner's diagonal tension field still carries shear, at the price of extra loads on the booms.
An open thin wall resists torque only through St Venant torsion, with stiffness proportional to t³, so closing the same material into a box raises torsional stiffness by orders of magnitude.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine a sketch of the cut section, the shear-flow integration from a free edge or the cut loop, and an explicit compatibility statement (zero twist, equal twist, or known shear centre) before any numbers are put in.

bank.q: Define shear flow and shear centre. Explain, with a sketch, why a transverse load acting through the shear centre bends the beam without twisting it, and why a load offset from it adds a torque.
outline: Write q = τt with units N/mm and state that q acts along the wall centreline.
Define shear centre as the point where the resultant of the shear flows acts, so the twisting moment about it is zero.
Show that a load offset by e from the shear centre gives torque T = Pe, which the section must react by torsion.
Sketch a channel section with the shear centre outside the web, on the opposite side to the flanges.

bank.q: Starting from a free edge, explain how the shear flow distribution in an open thin-walled section is obtained, and write the expression for q in terms of the applied shear force and the section second moments.
outline: State that q = 0 at a free edge because no shear can cross the free boundary.

Write q<sub>s</sub> = −(S<sub>x</sub>I<sub>xx</sub> − S<sub>y</sub>I<sub>xy</sub>)/(I<sub>xx</sub>I<sub>yy</sub> − I<sub>xy</sub>²)∫t x ds − (similar term in y) ds, and define S<sub>x</sub>, S<sub>y</sub>, I<sub>xx</sub>, I<sub>yy</sub>, I<sub>xy</sub>, s.
For a symmetric section simplify to q = −(S<sub>y</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub>)∫t y ds.
Explain that the integral accumulates the direct stress gradient from the free edge.
Note that the shear flow is statically determinate: no compatibility equation is needed.

bank.q: State and explain the Bredt-Batho theory for torsion of a closed thin-walled tube. Give the expressions for the shear flow, the shear stress, the rate of twist and the torsion constant.
outline: State the assumptions: thin wall, constant thickness round a loop, no warping restraint, shear flow uniform round the loop.
Give q = T/(2A) and τ = T/(2At), defining A as the area enclosed by the wall centreline and t as thickness.
Give dθ/dz = T/(GJ) with J = 4A²/∮(ds/t), and the total twist θ = TL/(GJ) over length L.
Explain physically why the enclosed area, not the perimeter alone, dominates the stiffness.

bank.q: Explain structural idealization of a wing section into booms and panels. State what each part carries, and why the idealized section gives nearly the same answer as the real one.
outline: Replace each stringer plus its share of skin by a boom of area B carrying all direct stress.
Replace the skin between booms by a panel carrying only shear flow, uniform along the panel.
Justify the split: the skin is thin, so its direct stress resultant is small compared with the concentrated areas.
Show the reduction of a wall integral to a sum over booms, and note that boom areas can include a correction for skin carrying direct stress.

bank.q: A thin-walled open channel section of uniform thickness t carries a vertical shear force S. Derive the shear flow round the section, sketch its distribution, and locate the shear centre.
outline: Take a cut at a free edge and integrate the direct stress gradient along the flanges and web.
Evaluate q at each corner and along each wall, showing the parabolic variation in the web and linear variation in the flanges.
Take moments of the shear flows about a convenient point in the web to find the line of action of the resultant.
Report the shear centre position as a distance from the web, and check that it lies outside the section for a channel.

bank.q: A single-cell closed section is made by closing a channel with a thin wall. Using the cut-and-add method, find the basic shear flow q<sub>b</sub>, determine the constant q₀ from the condition that the section twists by the correct amount, and hence locate the shear centre.
outline: Cut the loop at a convenient point to make an open section; compute q<sub>b</sub> from the free-edge integration.
Add a constant q₀ to all walls so the true shear flow is q = q<sub>b</sub> + q₀.
Apply the condition of zero twist rate for a shear force through the shear centre: ∮(q/t)ds = 0, or the equivalent moment condition.
Solve for q₀, then take moments of the resulting shear flows to find the shear centre.
State the sign convention used for q and for s round the loop.

bank.q: A closed thin-walled tube of given mean perimeter, wall thickness and enclosed area carries a torque T. Find the shear flow, the maximum shear stress, the rate of twist and the total angle of twist over a given length.
outline: Compute A from the mean dimensions and apply q = T/(2A).
Compute τ = q/t and identify where t is smallest for maximum stress.
Compute J = 4A²/∮(ds/t), summing ds/t over the walls of differing thickness.
Use θ = TL/(GJ) and dθ/dz = T/(GJ); state units of radians and G in N/mm².

bank.q: A two-cell wing box carries a pure torque T. Set up and solve the equations for the shear flows q₁ and q₂ in the two cells, and find the rate of twist.
outline: Write the torque equation T = 2A₁q₁ + 2A₂q₂ using the enclosed area of each cell.
Write the equal-twist equation for the shared wall: (1/2A₁G)∮₁(q/t)ds = (1/2A₂G)∮₂(q/t)ds, with the shared wall contributing to both integrals.
Solve the two simultaneous equations for q₁ and q₂, taking care with the sign of the shear flow in the common wall.
Compute the common twist rate from either cell and check both give the same value.

bank.q: An idealized wing section has four booms of given areas and thin panels of given lengths. For a vertical shear force, compute the shear flow in each panel and the boom direct stresses.
outline: Confirm the section is open at a chosen free edge, so q starts at zero.
Use q<sub>b</sub> = −(S<sub>y</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub>)Σ B y over the booms passed from the cut, summing contributions one boom at a time.
Compute I<sub>xx</sub> from the boom areas and their y distances, ignoring the thin panels.
Tabulate the shear flow in each panel and check it returns to zero at the far free edge.
Compute boom stresses from σ = M<sub>x</sub>y/I<sub>xx</sub>.

bank.q: A tapered beam or tapered wing carries a shear force and bending moment at one station. Derive and evaluate the additional taper shear flow caused by the spanwise component of the boom loads.
outline: Note that in a tapered beam the boom axial load P changes along the span, so the boom has a spanwise resultant component.
Resolve this change of boom load into components along and normal to the beam axis.
Add the normal component as an extra concentrated load at each boom and re-evaluate the shear flow it produces.
Add this taper shear flow to the ordinary bending shear flow to get the total.
Show that the taper contribution vanishes when the taper angle is zero.

bank.q: A section mixes one closed cell with an open flange outstand. Explain how many cuts and how many constants q₀ are needed, and write the compatibility conditions that determine them.
outline: Cut each closed cell once and also start the open part at its free edge; compute q<sub>b</sub> for the resulting open section.
Introduce one constant q₀ per cell; the open part takes no constant.
Write one equation per cell from the known twist rate (zero for a shear load through the shear centre, or T/(GJ) for a pure torque).
Write the torque balance over all cells and the open walls to close the set.
Solve the linear system, then superpose to get the true shear flow in every wall.

bank.q: Compare an open thin-walled section, a single closed box and a multi-cell box of the same material and roughly the same overall size for use as a wing torque box. Evaluate the torsional stiffness, the stress levels and the penalty of adding internal walls.
outline: Show that the open section resists torque only by St Venant torsion, with J = Σ(bt³/3), so stiffness scales with t³.
Show that the closed single cell has J = 4A²/∮(ds/t), which scales with A² and is far larger for the same wall thickness.
Explain that a multi-cell box spreads the shear flow over more walls, lowers the peak stress, but adds weight and manufacturing cost.
Conclude why real wings use closed multi-cell boxes and why open sections appear only where torsion is small.

bank.q: A thin web between two booms has buckled in shear. Using Wagner's diagonal tension field concept, explain how the web still carries shear and how the shear flows and boom loads are found.
outline: Describe the diagonal tension field: tension along one diagonal, compression along the other, at an angle α to the boom axis.
State that the web carries shear by the diagonal stress field, so the effective shear flow depends on α.
Write the equilibrium of a web panel to relate the applied shear flow to the diagonal tension and to the extra axial load transferred to the booms.
Explain that the total boom load is the bending load plus the diagonal tension contribution, and that α is found from compatibility of the boom and web extensions.
Note the design consequence: a buckled web is still a load path, but the booms must be sized for the extra axial load.

bank.q: Discuss the assumptions behind Bredt-Batho theory and behind boom-panel idealization, and evaluate the situations in which each one gives a misleading answer for a real aircraft wing.
outline: List Bredt-Batho assumptions: thin wall, closed loop, uniform shear flow, no warping restraint, elastic behaviour.
List idealization assumptions: booms carry all direct stress, panels carry only shear, direct stress constant along a panel.
Identify where they fail: thick or abrupt joints, cut-outs and access holes, restrained warping at wing root, post-buckled skin, tapering.
Recommend when a finite element check or a more refined model is needed.
Conclude that the closed-form results are design tools whose limits must be checked.

glossary.def: The shear force transmitted per unit length along a thin wall, equal to shear stress times wall thickness and measured in N/mm.
The point in a cross-section through which a transverse load must pass for the section to bend without twisting.
Another name for the shear centre, stressing that it is the point where the bending shear flows have their resultant.
A section whose wall thickness is small compared with its overall width and depth, so shear stress can be taken as uniform through the thickness.
A section whose wall centreline does not close on itself, such as a channel, angle or Z-section.
A section whose wall centreline forms one or more closed loops, such as a box or a tube.
The shear flow obtained in a closed section after it is cut open, before the constant loop shear flow is added.
An imaginary slit made in a closed loop so that the free-edge shear flow integration can be started.
An equation on deformation, such as zero twist or equal twist in all cells, used to find the unknown constant shear flows.
The angle of twist per unit length, dθ/dz = T/(GJ), in radians per millimetre.
The thin-walled closed-tube torsion theory in which the shear flow is constant round the loop and equals T/(2A).
The area bounded by the centreline of a closed wall, used in the Bredt-Batho formulas and in the torsion constant.
The geometric quantity J in T = GJ(dθ/dz), equal to 4A²/∮(ds/t) for a closed cell and Σ(bt³/3) for an open wall.
Out-of-plane displacement of the cross-section when a non-circular section twists, which is restrained at a built-in end.
A closed section made of two or more adjacent closed loops sharing common internal walls, typical of a wing torsion box.
A concentrated area in an idealized section that carries all the direct stress from bending.
A thin wall of an idealized section lying between two booms and carrying only shear flow.
The axial force in a boom, equal to its direct stress times its area, used to find the taper shear flow.
The gradual change of cross-section size along a beam or wing, measured as the angle between the outer surface and the beam axis.
The pattern of diagonal tension and compression in a thin web that has buckled in shear, still able to carry load.
A web designed to carry shear without buckling, usually by being thick or closely stiffened.
Pure torsion of a bar with free warping, whose stiffness for a thin open wall is proportional to the cube of the wall thickness.
The geometric property I = ∫y²dA of a section about an axis, which sets the bending direct stress and the shear flow magnitude.
